title: The body as a boat
hook: a twelve-step skincare routine on one side, four hours of sleep and cold pizza on the other; Shantideva says: a boat
tomorrow: how much good can a single flash of anger burn?

segments.voice: Yesterday, before moving: examine your mind before you move, speak or even glance. Check first. Today, the thing that does all the moving: the body itself.

Scroll for a minute and you'll see two kinds of people. One has a skincare routine with a dozen steps, a mirror selfie after every workout, a body that's become a full-time project. The other is running on four hours of sleep, cold pizza and a deadline, treating the body like a rental car they'll return someday. Both feel normal. So, yesterday's question: is the body something to worship, or something to use? Shantideva's answer is neither, exactly. It's a boat.
screen: `A BODY AS A PROJECT.` → `A BODY AS A RENTAL CAR.` → `WORSHIP IT, OR USE IT?`

segments.voice: Chapter five holds two views of the body, and both are honest Buddhist voices. View one: don't make it an idol. Shantideva asks the reader to look closely at the body, skin, flesh, bone, and to see that there's nothing in it worth clinging to as if it were the whole point. Why guard it so jealously, he asks, when it will be left behind? The best case for this view: it frees you. A body that isn't an idol can age, scar and change without your whole self going down with it. View two: don't wreck it. The same chapter says the body that carries the teaching shouldn't be harmed for some small reason. And elsewhere the poem calls this human life hard to find. The best case here: a body you starve and exhaust can't help anyone, including you. Then Shantideva brings the two together in one picture. Regard the body as a boat, he says, simply a support for coming and going, used for the good of beings. A boat isn't worshipped. Nobody burns incense to the hull. But nobody sails a boat with holes in it either. You patch it, you bail it out, and you take it somewhere that matters.
screen: `VIEW ONE: NOT AN IDOL.` · `VIEW TWO: DON'T WRECK IT.` · `A SUPPORT FOR COMING AND GOING.` · `PATCH IT, AND SAIL.` · then, large: `A BOAT, NOT AN IDOL.`

segments.voice: Take a glass of water, or anything plain to drink, and hold it a moment before you sip. Taste it slowly, feel it go down, and notice the body receiving something simple and good. That's patching the boat: no fuss, no neglect.
The body as a boat: Shantideva's way through. Not worshipped, not wrecked, but cared for and used to carry good across.
screen: `THE BODY AS A BOAT — today's word`.

segments.voice: A line for the day: a boat, not an idol, patched and sailing. That's chapter five's watchfulness, wrapped up.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers hold together two teachings on the body: reflecting on its impermanence so it isn't clung to, and valuing a human life as a rare chance to practice; monastic rules include care for health, food and medicine.

fork.setup: your friend is training for a race and runs through a painful injury because 'pain is weakness leaving.' in Shantideva's two views, which best case fits?
options: view one: the body isn't the point, so ignore the pain and push on.
view two: don't harm the boat for a small reason; rest it and sail later.
neither: the body should be pampered so it never feels pain at all.
fork.reveal: not clinging to the body doesn't mean wrecking it. Shantideva says not to harm it for a small reason; a boat with holes sails nowhere.

original.note: Sanskrit: boat, ship (nau). Shantideva asks the reader to think of the body as a boat.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhists either ignore the body or punish it.
what it means: Shantideva treats the body as a boat: not worshipped, not wrecked, cared for and used for others' good.
what a scholar hears: chapter five sets reflection on the body's impurity beside the rule not to harm it for trivial reasons; the boat verse joins the two.
guess: caring for the body and using it for good, not clinging
a body trained hard until it can carry heavy loads
an old belief that the body floats after you die

chat.says: skipped dinner three nights for the mural. mom's upset. isn't sacrifice kind of the point?
options: Not this kind. The body's your boat for the mural. Eat, then paint.
Yes. Real artists suffer. Your mom will get it once the mural is done.
Maybe skip painting instead, since the body is the most important thing.
chat.meaning: Shantideva: the body is a boat, not an idol, and not to be harmed for small reasons. A sinking boat carries nothing.

Shantideva.meaning: Buddhist poet-monk who wrote this guide to the bodhisattva's way

idol.meaning: here, something treated as the whole point of life

incense.meaning: fragrant sticks burned as an offering at shrines

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 5.60-5.70 (examining the body, nothing to cling to; regard the body as a boat, a support for coming and going, for the good of beings) and 5.86-5.87 (the body that serves the true dharma should not be harmed for a trivial reason)
Bodhicaryavatara 1.4 (this human life, with its freedoms, is very hard to find)
